721.quote_or_event: “A monk should be modest though he be of a fearless mind; he should expound the Syâdvâda; he should use the two (permitted) kinds of speech, living among virtuous men, impartial and wise.”
721.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on the Nirgrantha tells the teaching monk to pair a fearless mind with modesty, to speak in the qualified, many-sided manner of syadvada, and to use only the permitted kinds of speech.
721.tie_back: The Kural's pure-minded speaker who knows the full range of words and does not stumble before a powerful assembly matches this monk, who is fearless yet modest and weighs every word he speaks among others.
721.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
721._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It closely matches fearless, disciplined speech, but the Jain verse says nothing about first sizing up what kind of assembly one faces.

722.quote_or_event: “(If the pupil does not understand his short explanation), he should explain at greater length. When the pupil has heard it, he will correctly understand the Truth.”
722.explanation: The same lecture tells the teacher to fit his explanation to the hearer and to lengthen it when a short account does not get through, so that the listener really grasps the truth.
722.tie_back: The Kural praises those who speak so that their learning actually reaches the hearers; the Jain teacher is likewise judged by whether his words reach and settle in the listener.
722.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
722._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It is strong on making teaching reach the hearer, but the setting is a teacher and pupil, not a learned assembly, and the Kural's 'most learned of the learned' ranking is missing.

723.quote_or_event: “Monks who equal the ocean in depth, who are difficult to overcome, are frightened by nobody (or nothing), and are not easily assailed, who are full of extensive learning and take care of themselves, will go to the highest place, after their Karman has been annihilated.”
723.explanation: The lecture 'The Very Learned' compares the learned monk to heroes, kings and the ocean, and closes by naming fearlessness ('frightened by nobody') as a mark of deep learning.
723.tie_back: The Kural says fearless speakers in an assembly are rarer than men willing to die among enemies; the Jain text also holds fearlessness joined to learning to be a rare and high attainment.
723.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
723._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It shares the pairing of learning and fearlessness, but it lacks the Kural's sharp contrast between battlefield courage and courage in an assembly.

724.quote_or_event: “At the right time he may put a question about living beings to a well-conducted (monk), who will explain the conduct of the virtuous; and what he hears he should follow and treasure up in his heart, thinking that it is the doctrine of the Kêvalins.”
724.explanation: The Nirgrantha lecture asks the monk both to teach others (I.14.5) and to go to better-informed monks with his questions, keeping what he learns from them.
724.tie_back: The Kural's twofold duty, to present one's learning before the learned and then take from those who know more, matches the Jain monk who teaches yet keeps learning from his superiors.
724.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.15; cf. I.14.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
724._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The learn-from-those-who-know half fits well, but the Jain verse is about monastic instruction rather than speaking in an assembly.

725.quote_or_event: “The knowledge (of the seven categories) is attained by means of pramāṇa and naya.”
725.explanation: Umasvati makes valid means of knowledge (pramana) and partial standpoints (naya) the method for knowing reality, and Pujyapada's commentary adds that pramana is 'for oneself' and 'for others', with knowledge put into words serving as pramana for others.
725.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads this Kural as urging study of the science of pramana, logic, so as to answer without fear in an assembly; Jainism makes that same science of pramana and naya the basis of all sound knowledge and argument.
725.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
725._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Pramana as the means of valid knowledge fits the commentators' reading of this Kural well, though the sutra is about knowing the categories of reality, not about debate.

726.quote_or_event: “As a trained Kambôga-steed, whom no noise frightens, exceeds all other horses in speed, so a very learned monk is superior to all others.”
726.explanation: In praising the very learned monk, the Uttaradhyayana chooses a war-horse that no noise can frighten, so fearlessness becomes part of what makes learning excel.
726.tie_back: The Kural asks what use books are to someone who fears a sharp assembly; the Jain simile likewise counts learning as excellent only when it comes with steady nerve.
726.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
726._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Learning and fearlessness are joined in one image, but there is no counterpart to the Kural's pairing of a sword with books.

727.quote_or_event: “As at the time of the battle the coward looks behind him for a ditch, thicket, or other hiding-place, (thinking that) nobody knows who will win; 'A moment's moment will bring the decision; when we lose, we shall fly.' Thus thinks the coward.”
727.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the coward who plans his escape in battle as a picture of weak monks who, when tested, fall back on worldly skills instead of standing firm.
727.tie_back: The Kural's learned man who fears the assembly is like a sharp sword in a coward's hand before the enemy; the Jain text uses the same coward-in-battle figure for someone whose equipment is wasted by lack of nerve.
727.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.3.1-2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
727._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The coward-in-battle image is shared, but the Jain passage is about a monk's resolve under hardship, not about learning wasted through fear of an assembly, and it has no sword simile.

728.quote_or_event: “Therefore, seeker after the highest truth, study the sacred lore, in order to cause yourself and others to attain perfection.”
728.explanation: The closing verse of 'The Very Learned' says the purpose of study is the good of others as well as oneself.
728.tie_back: The Kural says many subjects studied are useless if one cannot put them well before a good assembly; the Jain verse similarly holds that learning is meant to benefit others, not only its owner.
728.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
728._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: the verse shares the idea that learning should serve others but does not call learning useless when it is not communicated.

729.quote_or_event: “Weak men who are unable (to bear) these insults in villages or towns, become disheartened like cowards in the battle.”
729.explanation: Among the troubles of monastic life, the Sutrakritanga lists public ridicule in villages and towns, and says weak monks give way under it like cowards in battle.
729.tie_back: The Kural ranks the learned man who dreads a good assembly below the unlearned; the Jain verse likewise treats losing one's nerve before the public as a real failure in someone who has taken up the higher life.
729.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
729._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: it condemns giving way before people's insults, but it says nothing about learning and makes no comparison with the unlearned.

730.quote_or_event: “Those who having investigated the Law expound it, are awakened and put an end to mundane existence; able to liberate both (themselves and others), they answer the well-deliberated questions.”
730.explanation: The Nirgrantha lecture praises those who have studied the doctrine and then expound it, answering questions so that both they and others are freed.
730.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot pass on what they learned are like the dead; the Jain verse puts the same value the other way round, praising those who do expound their learning as fully awakened.
730.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
730._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It is the positive counterpart of the Kural's point, but it has no 'living dead' image and does not mention fear of the assembly.
